activities.anchor: Read separately, each one misleads in a characteristic way
activities.caption: pair each statement with its question
activities.name: fsStatementsMatch

config.prompt: Three frozen frames of one process — pair each statement with the question it answers:

pairs.right: how did the business perform over this period?
what does it own and owe right now?
the model, the health — and sometimes the crimes

config.why: Each statement misleads in a characteristic way on its own: the income statement reflects choices, the balance sheet freezes an instant, the cash flow statement fact-checks both.

activities.anchor: runs one line at a time down to the bottom
activities.caption: rebuild the staircase, top line to bottom line
activities.name: fsStaircaseOrder

config.prompt: The income statement's staircase — rebuild it in order:
items: Revenue — the top line: what customers were charged
Subtract COGS (materials, direct labour) to reach gross profit
Subtract operating expenses (salaries, rent, R&D, depreciation) to reach operating profit (EBIT)
Subtract interest, settle tax — the bottom line: net income
config.why: The staircase structure is the point: you can see where profit was made or lost, not just how much — gross margin is the purest read on pricing power, from software's 70–80 cents to the grocer's 2–3.

activities.anchor: a retailer sells for 100, having bought the goods for 60
activities.caption: bet before you read on — the margin squeeze
activities.name: fsMarginPredict

config.q: The worked retailer: gross margin 40 per cent, net income 9. A 5-point squeeze in gross margin hits. What happens to profit?
choices: More than halved — thin-margin operating leverage
config.why: Gross profit falls from 40 to 35 and nearly all of it drops through: profit goes from 9 to well under half. A 5-point squeeze more than halves profit — the operating leverage of thin-margin businesses.

activities.anchor: bound by the identity that never fails
activities.caption: fill the identity — and its inventor
activities.name: fsIdentityCloze

config.text: The identity that never fails: Assets = %%0%% + Equity. Every transaction touches it twice — double-entry bookkeeping, invented by %%1%% in %%2%% — which is what gives accounts their self-checking arithmetic.
config.hint: The residual's partner, the friar, and the year.

activities.anchor: Every dollar that entered or left is classified into three streams
activities.caption: file the cash-flow diagnosis
activities.name: fsStreamsBuckets

config.prompt: The layout reads like a diagnosis — file each sign:

items.label: investing negative because it builds — buying its future
financing swings either way while operations carry it
weak operating cash flow patched by borrowing
profits that never arrive as cash

config.why: Negative investing cash flow is normal for a healthy growing company; the patient to worry about is the one whose operating stream cannot fund itself.

activities.anchor: The key professional metric hides here
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the conversion note
activities.name: fsConversionSpot

config.prompt: One line of this analyst's note is wrong — click it:
lines: Cash conversion is operating cash flow divided by net income.
Persistently below 1 means profits that never arrive as cash.
Sales booked to customers who don't pay show up as rising receivables.
Enron's reported billions were backed by equally strong operating cash flow.
Profit is an opinion, cash is a fact — the cliché keeps being true.
config.correction: Enron's operating cash flow quietly deteriorated before the 2001 collapse — the accruals had to be manufactured, and they were.
config.why: Cash conversion below 1 is the classic early warning: costs capitalised instead of expensed, growth drowning in receivables.

activities.anchor: Watch the chain work in one transaction
activities.caption: one sale, three statements — line up the journey
activities.name: fsChainOrder

config.prompt: One sale of 100, costing 60, all on credit — line up the three statements' story:
items: Balance sheet: inventory down 60, receivables up 100 — assets rose 40
That 40 flows into equity via retained earnings
Cash flow statement shows nothing yet — no money moved
The customer pays: receivables fall 100, cash rises 100
config.why: One sale, three statements, one consistent story — and a fast-growing company can report soaring profit while its cash position worsens every quarter, because growth itself consumes working capital.

activities.caption: scrub the record — bookkeeping to quality-of-earnings
activities.name: fsEarningsTimeline

events.text: Luca Pacioli publishes the self-checking arithmetic every account still runs on.

events.title: Sloan's accruals anomaly
events.text: Firms with high accruals systematically underperform later — the market over-extrapolates pretty accrual earnings.

events.title: Enron collapses
events.text: Billions of reported net income while operating cash flow quietly deteriorated.

events.title: WorldCom exposed
events.text: Ordinary line costs treated as capital investments, inflating profit by billions.
